content:
It isn’t necessarily a recession indicator when cinema resorts to 19th-century IP, but the raft of recent Victor Hugo and Alexandre Dumas adaptations (“The Count of Monte Cristo,” “The Three Musketeers,” “Les Misérables”) surely doesn’t point to a resolutely confident industry either. Now a new film joins these ranks, as director Jean-François Richet and star Vincent Cassel team up once again for “The Hunchback, Soul of Paris,” a bag-securing adventure set within what we must unfortunately term “the extended Victor Hugoniverse.”
For this acts as a prequel to the events of the famous Hugo novel, which has spawned countless adaptations: The author himself appears as a character (don’t ask), as does a new iteration of Gavroche from “Les Mis.” As the film begins, a voiceover explains sententiously that, at a time when the king of France had recently brought in new laws to crush civil liberties, Quasimodo (Cassel) stands as “a man of the people… a man to represent the scorned and crushed populace.”
But first we must meet the fellow, who at the outset is straitjacketed in a hospice dealing with an outbreak of cholera, where the superintendent doctor (Benjamin Voisin, clocking in for work) believes that the hunchback holds the key to a vaccine, as he is miraculously resistant to the illness. Quasimodo escapes thanks to his superhuman strength (of which more later) and takes refuge within the cathedral, his blue eye reflecting the building’s vast rose window before we surge over the ancient city for a money-flaunting title card. Pa-dam! The stakes are set!
At this stage it’s instructive to remember that both Cassel and Richet originally came to the fore with urgent dramas (“La Haine” and “Ma 6-T Va Crack-er”) set in the cités of Parisian suburbs, which sounded popular unrest among France’s dispossessed, chiefly immigrant communities. “The Hunchback, Soul of Paris” ostensibly sides with the people but its approach is perhaps a little less than strictly Marxist-Leninist, as Richet uses his vast budget to indulge in every period drama trope under the sun.
Adopting a formidable declension of every colour from sepia to brown, Richet depicts light streaming through dusty windows; moaning invalids with sores; plucky street urchins; an olde laboratory; a bawdy sex-worker; grimy cobbled streets galore of course; and last but not least, an opulent dinner party, filmed in flat shot/reverse shot, during which two men debate the ethical implications of scientific advancement over the port course. A sure sign of the film’s ambient bourgeoisie comes in its treatment of Notre-Dame itself, which we first encounter as an exceptionally hallowed place filled with spiritual light from on high as angelic choirs warble impossibly high notes: Here, you see, is the soul of Paris.
But back to the young doctor, who, you see, believes it is advisable to use the less fortunate in order to benefit science, and to this end orders that Quasimodo be brought to him by hook or by crook, enlisting the help of the corrupt police chief Coco-Lacour (played by Karim Leklou with remarkable commitment and finesse, where a much less engaged performance would have sufficed). There ensues — and this is really quite baffling — an almost total lack of plot development for the best part of an hour. Instead, we meet Agnès (Daphné Patakia), a young and gutsy street performer with whom Quasimodo falls in love, prefiguring Esmeralda, and observe the titular hunchback as he defends her, scurries around, and lugs huge blocks of marble about the place.
In one of the film’s big ideas, Quasimodo is depicted as having superhuman strength, which situates this story about scientists wanting to study his powers in the same lineage as “X-Men” and “Captain America.” One suspects that dimension won’t send Gen-Z flocking, and it is a rather tired formula overall, giving a handful of fight scenes a wearisome sense of déjà vu as the guys getting punched skid a good three further meters along the ground than you might expect.
As events very slowly begin to grind towards a climactic confrontation, Cassel seems hampered by the main character’s make-up and lack of characterization, his performance reduced to a mere bodily incarnation of the hunchback. (A late scene in which he stammeringly bonds with Agnès, on a high rampart atop the cathedral, is perfectly risible and symptomatic of a much wider problem with character-building.) Patakia, as the somewhat modern-minded tart with a heart, is appealing and sensitive enough, but the role is paper-thin. At last, the capturing of Quasimodo sparks a skirmish and Paris starts to burn, but even here Richet feels uninspired, and the battle scenes — while handsomely art-directed — lack energy and pizzazz. It’s left to Patakia, in a bonnet and décolleté, to mirror Eugène Delacroix’s “Liberty Leading the People,” in a rather mortifying slow-mo that encapsulates the film’s general vanity and lack of inspiration.
